subject: computer-science
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: In a 2D array declared as A[rows][columns], element A[2][3] refers to:
options: The element at row index 2, column index 3
questions.explain: A 2D array is indexed by row then column, so A[2][3] is the cell at row 2, column 3.

questions.q: A 'good' hash function should ideally:
options: Map all keys to the same index
Depend on the table never being resized
Distribute keys uniformly across the table to minimise collisions
questions.explain: A good hash function spreads keys evenly to reduce collisions and keep lookups efficient.

questions.q: A pre-order traversal of a binary tree visits nodes in which order?
questions.explain: Pre-order visits the root first, then the left subtree, then the right subtree.

questions.q: In a binary search tree, for any given node, values in its left subtree are:
questions.explain: In a BST, the left subtree contains values less than the node and the right subtree values greater.

questions.q: A weighted graph is one in which:
options: Each edge carries a numerical value such as a cost or distance
Every vertex has the same number of edges
questions.explain: In a weighted graph each edge has an associated weight representing cost, distance or similar.

questions.q: What is the key difference between a static and a dynamic data structure?
options: Static structures must use linked lists
Static structures can grow at run time; dynamic ones cannot
A static structure has a fixed size set at compile time, while a dynamic one can grow or shrink at run time
questions.explain: Static structures (e.g. arrays) have fixed size, whereas dynamic structures (e.g. linked lists) change size during execution.

questions.q: A post-order traversal of a binary tree visits nodes in which order?
questions.explain: Post-order visits the left subtree, then the right subtree, then the root last.

questions.q: Traversing a linked list means:
options: Following each node's pointer in turn from the head to visit every node
questions.explain: Traversal starts at the head and follows the next pointers to visit every node in sequence.

questions.q: Why is a stack described as the structure that enables backtracking, such as the 'undo' feature?
options: Because the most recent action is on top and is the first to be reversed
Because it serves items in arrival order
Because it uses a hash function
questions.explain: A stack's LIFO behaviour means the last action performed is the first one undone.

questions.q: For a graph with few edges (sparse), which representation is generally more memory efficient?
options: Two-dimensional array of all vertex pairs
questions.explain: An adjacency list stores only existing edges, so it is more space efficient than a matrix for sparse graphs.

questions.q: A queue is an abstract data type that operates on which principle?
questions.explain: A queue is FIFO: items leave in the same order they were added.

questions.q: A stack is an abstract data type that operates on which principle?
questions.explain: A stack is LIFO: the most recently pushed item is the first one popped.

questions.q: A queue is the most appropriate structure for which of the following uses?
options: Buffering data such as a print job spooler
questions.explain: A FIFO queue suits buffering, where items are processed in the order they arrive, e.g. a print spooler.

questions.q: In a singly linked list, each node typically stores:
options: Data and a pointer to the next node
A pointer to the previous node only
questions.explain: A singly linked list node holds its data and a pointer (reference) to the next node in the list.

questions.q: An in-order traversal of a binary search tree visits the nodes in what order of values?
questions.explain: In-order traversal of a BST (left, root, right) yields the keys in ascending sorted order.

questions.q: In a priority queue, items are dequeued based on:
options: Their assigned priority, with highest priority served first
Alphabetical order of the structure name
The order they were inserted only
questions.explain: A priority queue removes the highest-priority element first, regardless of insertion order.

questions.q: Attempting to pop from an empty stack causes which condition?
questions.explain: Removing from an empty stack is a stack underflow; adding beyond capacity is overflow.

questions.q: Which data structure is most naturally used to evaluate a reverse Polish (postfix) expression?
questions.explain: A stack handles postfix evaluation by pushing operands and popping them when an operator is met.

questions.q: Which data structure is used internally to manage the sequence of subroutine calls and returns (recursion)?
questions.explain: The call stack stores return addresses and local data for each active subroutine call in LIFO order.

questions.q: Which two operations add to and remove from a stack respectively?
questions.explain: push adds an item to the top of a stack and pop removes the item from the top.

questions.q: Chaining is a collision-resolution technique in which:
options: The key is rehashed until the table is full
The table is resized on every insertion
Items are stored in a stack
Each table slot holds a linked list of all items hashing to that index
questions.explain: With chaining, each bucket stores a linked list of entries that share the same hash index.

questions.q: In a circular queue, what advantage does it have over a simple linear queue using an array?
options: It reuses freed space at the front by wrapping the rear pointer around
It removes the need for a front pointer
questions.explain: A circular queue wraps the rear pointer to the start, reusing slots vacated by dequeued items.

questions.q: In a doubly linked list, each node differs from a singly linked list node by also storing:
options: A pointer to the previous node
questions.explain: A doubly linked list node holds pointers to both the next and the previous nodes, allowing two-way traversal.

questions.q: In an adjacency matrix representing a graph of n vertices, the space required is proportional to:
questions.explain: An adjacency matrix is an n by n grid, so it uses space proportional to n squared.

questions.q: A hash table resolves the situation where two keys hash to the same index; this situation is called a:
questions.explain: A collision occurs when the hash function maps two different keys to the same slot.

questions.q: In an undirected graph, an edge between vertices A and B means:
options: A has higher priority than B
A and B are the same vertex
You can travel only from A to B
There is a connection that can be traversed in both directions
questions.explain: In an undirected graph edges have no direction, so the connection works both ways.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of the 'rear' and 'front' pointers in a queue implemented with an array?
options: To store the queue's data values
To mark where items are added (rear) and removed (front)
questions.explain: The rear pointer indicates where the next enqueue occurs and the front where the next dequeue occurs.

questions.q: A binary tree node may have at most how many children?
questions.explain: By definition each node of a binary tree has at most two children (left and right).

questions.q: To insert a new node between two existing nodes in a linked list, you must:
options: Update the pointers so the previous node points to the new node and the new node points to the following node
Recompute a hash for every node
Shift all subsequent elements one place along
questions.explain: Insertion in a linked list only requires repointing the surrounding nodes' pointers, no shifting of elements.

questions.q: Which statement about an array is true compared with a linked list?
options: An array can only be traversed via pointers
An array allows direct (random) indexed access to any element in constant time
An array is always dynamic in size
questions.explain: Arrays support O(1) random access by index, whereas a linked list must be traversed sequentially.
